abstract: Microeukaryotes are a diverse and functionally important component of river biofilms, including primary producers, consumers, decomposers, and parasites and symbionts. However, their diversity is likely underestimated, and their composition, environmental drivers, and seasonal dynamics have rarely been studied at large spatial scales. Microbiological monitoring of freshwater ecosystems has historically focused almost entirely on diatoms, so the potential of the wider microbial community as indicators of river condition is unknown. Here, we used 18S rRNA gene metabarcoding of more than 1,600 biofilm samples from 700 sites across England's River Surveillance Network. We show that communities were dominated by diatoms, chlorophytes, ciliates, and fungi, and shifted from phototroph-dominated biofilms in spring towards more diverse, heterotroph-rich biofilms in autumn. Community turnover was driven by water chemistry rather than geographic distance, with alkalinity, DO, temperature, and nitrate-N among the strongest drivers of composition. Co-occurrence networks resolved assemblages of taxa with shared environmental responses, and threshold indicator taxa analysis identified ASV-level indicators of water chemistry gradients. Community change points along these gradients closely matched those reported for bacteria from the same biofilms, and several taxa declined at lower concentrations than the community as a whole, offering potential early warning of change. These findings show that the microeukaryotic community tracks water chemistry consistently across a national river network and can provide a taxonomically broad set of sensitive and interpretable indicators of river condition that complement diatom-based monitoring and emerging bacterial approaches.
